result:
As I sit here, staring out the window at the world going by, my mind begins to wander. It's a beautiful day, the sun is shining, and the birds are singing their sweet melodies. It's days like these that I'm reminded of just how fleeting life can be.

We're so caught up in our daily routines, our heads down, staring at our screens, and our feet moving in a robotic pace, that we forget to appreciate the little things. The way the light filters through the leaves, the sound of children's laughter, the smell of freshly cut grass.

But life isn't always as idyllic as it is today. There are moments of darkness, of struggle, of uncertainty. And it's in those moments that we must remind ourselves of the beauty of the world.

I think back to my childhood, spending countless hours exploring the woods behind my house. The rustle of leaves, the snap of twigs, the gentle streams that flowed through the underbrush. I was a curious child, always getting into trouble, but those were the days when the world seemed limitless, and the possibilities seemed endless.

And then I grew up. Responsibilities, jobs, relationships – all of which seemed to suck the magic out of the world. But it's interesting, because even as I was following the script of adulthood, I never lost the sense of wonder. I've always been one of those people who look at a sunset and feels a lump form in their throat. Who stands in awe of the stars, feeling the enormity of the universe stretching out before them.

I remember the first time I traveled to Europe. I must have been 19 or 20. I was backpacking through Italy, couch-surfing with fellow travelers, and eating my weight in pizza. It was exhilarating, to say the least. I felt like I was seeing the world for the first time, and everything seemed so new, so exciting.

And yet, even as I was wandering those cobblestone streets, I couldn't shake the feeling that there was more to life than what I was experiencing. It's funny, how our perceptions change as we grow older. When we're young, we're forced to navigate the world with our basic instincts intact – curiosity, courage, and a dash of recklessness. But as we age, those instincts get layered over with responsibilities, with fears, with doubts.

Don't get me wrong – I'm not trying to romanticize the past, or the innocence of youth. Adulthood is beautiful too, in its own, messy way. There's a sense of security, of belonging, of having duties and obligations that make us feel seen and valued. And yet, there's also a sense of detachment, of disconnection, of fragmentation.

As I wander through the world today, I'm struck by the way people seem to live in separate bubbles, their Facebook profiles a curated highlight reel of their happiness, their Instagram feeds a filtered facade of their achievements. We're more connected than ever, and yet, simultaneously more isolated. We have the world at our fingertips, and yet, we're unable to stay present in the moment.

I think this is what's so wonderful about travel. When we leave our familiar routines behind, and step into the unknown, something magical happens. Our senses come alive, our hearts open up, and our minds begin to expand. We're no longer just being, we're being-elsewhere. We're being-present, fully, and utterly, in the moment.

But it's not just about traveling, or seeing the world. It's about paying attention. It's about noticing the beauty in the everyday, the majesty in the mundane. It's about being small enough to see the world in its entirety.

As I write this, I'm reminded of a phrase my grandmother used to say. "You can't grieve what you don't love." She meant that we can't pour out our hearts for something we're not invested in. We can't lose what we've never truly found.

When was the last time you wept at the beauty of the world? I mean, truly wept? Not just for what we've lost, or sought, but for the majesty of the everyday? The way the light shines through the clouds, or the way the stars twinkle in the night sky?
